subject: geography
promptStrong: Give me a challenging KS3 geography question on {lo}, then mark my answer.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for KS3 simply, with an example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of PHYSICAL geography?
options: The main religion of a region
The number of people in a city
questions.explain: Physical geography is about natural features shaped by nature, such as valleys and mountains. Religion, population and jobs are all human geography — made or done by people.

questions.q: A student lists: climate, rivers, population, mountains. Which one is the odd one out because it is HUMAN geography?
questions.explain: Population is human geography (about people). Climate, rivers and mountains are all physical (natural) geography.

questions.q: Why do geographers use the SAME headings (climate, economy, population...) for each place they compare?
options: So the comparison is fair and like-for-like
questions.explain: Using the same headings lets you compare like-for-like — climate with climate, economy with economy — which is the only way to make a fair comparison.

questions.q: Which pair is a fair like-for-like comparison of two places?
options: Kenya's rainfall vs the UK's population
Kenya's main jobs vs the UK's main jobs
India's languages vs the UK's rivers
questions.explain: Comparing main jobs with main jobs uses the same heading (economy), so it is like-for-like. The other pairs mix different headings, which tells you nothing useful.

questions.q: The Nairobi region of Kenya lies close to the Equator. What is its climate mostly like?
options: Warm tropical highland with rainy seasons
Hot desert with almost no rain
Cool and changeable like the UK
questions.explain: Nairobi has a tropical highland climate — warm all year with two rainy seasons. Its high altitude keeps it milder than lowland places on the Equator.

questions.q: Kenya exports large amounts of tea, coffee and cut flowers. Which economic sector does this mainly belong to?
questions.explain: Growing crops like tea, coffee and flowers is farming, which is the primary sector — activities that take or grow natural resources from the land.

questions.q: Kerala, in southern India, receives very heavy rain from June to September. What is this rainy season called?
questions.explain: The heavy summer rains in South Asia are called the monsoon. They soak Kerala and are vital for growing rice and other crops.

questions.q: Kerala has a lower average income than the UK, but very high literacy and life expectancy. What does this best show?
options: Income alone can be misleading about development
Kerala is not really in Asia
Literacy does not matter for development
Kerala must be richer than the UK
questions.explain: One indicator like income can mislead. Kerala's high literacy and life expectancy show it is more developed than its income alone would suggest — so use several indicators.

questions.q: In London and the South-East of the UK, most people work in which economic sectors?
questions.explain: The UK is a developed economy where most jobs are in the tertiary and quaternary sectors — services, finance, media and technology — with very few people in farming.

questions.q: Compared with Nairobi, which statement about London's climate is correct?
options: London is cooler and more changeable (temperate)
questions.explain: London has a temperate maritime climate — cooler and more changeable, with rain spread through the year. Nairobi is warmer all year round.

questions.q: Which statement describes a SIMILARITY between Kenya and the UK?
options: Both have a warm tropical climate
Both have a large, fast-growing capital city
questions.explain: Both Kenya (Nairobi) and the UK (London) have a large, fast-growing capital city — a genuine similarity. Their climates and main jobs are differences.

questions.q: UK supermarkets sell cut flowers grown in Kenya. This is best described as which type of link between places?
questions.explain: Goods bought and sold between places are a trade link. Kenya's flowers being sold in the UK shows how the two places are connected through trade.

questions.q: Money sent home to families in Kerala by relatives working abroad is known as what?
questions.explain: Money sent home by migrant workers is called remittances. It is an important link created by migration and helps support Kerala's economy.

questions.q: Which of these is a development indicator used to compare places?
questions.explain: Life expectancy (how long people typically live) is a development indicator. Others include GDP per person and literacy rate. Physical features are not development measures.

questions.q: The Human Development Index (HDI) combines income with which two other things?
questions.explain: The HDI combines wealth (income), health (life expectancy) and education (schooling) into a single score from 0 to 1, giving a fuller picture than income alone.

questions.q: Why is it wrong to say 'Kenya is just like the rest of Africa'?
options: A region is not a whole continent — Africa is huge and varied
All of Africa has the same climate
questions.explain: A region or country is not a whole continent. Africa has 54 countries with enormous variety — deserts, rainforests, rich and poor areas — so Kenya cannot stand for all of it.

questions.q: A student says two places are 'completely different in every way'. Why is this usually a weak geographical claim?
options: Almost every pair of places has both similarities AND differences
questions.explain: Places almost always share some similarities and some differences at the same time. Saying they are different 'in every way' ignores the similarities and is an oversimplification.

questions.q: Nairobi has a growing technology industry ('Silicon Savannah') and Kerala has very high literacy. What does this teach us?
options: Developing regions can lead in some things, so avoid stereotypes
Only the UK can have technology
questions.explain: Developing regions can be world-leading in some areas. Judging places on evidence, not stereotypes, gives a fairer and more accurate comparison.
